summary: This standards-track document specifies how Ethernet VPN can be used as a network virtualization overlay for data centers. It examines tunnel encapsulation options over IP, including VXLAN, NVGRE and MPLS over GRE, and how they affect the EVPN control plane and procedures.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8365 describes how Ethernet VPN (EVPN) can connect separate tenant networks across shared IP infrastructure. It explains how tunnel choices affect route information, multihoming, and traffic between data centers.

subtitle: Using EVPN to carry tenant traffic over VXLAN, NVGRE, and MPLS-over-GRE overlays.

tldr.problem: A data center needs separate tenant networks over shared IP infrastructure, while supporting many tenants, Layer 2 reach, and movement of virtual machines.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC uses EVPN's BGP control plane with IP tunnel encapsulations. It maps virtual network identifiers into EVPN routes and defines how multihoming features work when the tunnel does not carry an MPLS label stack.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8365 specifies EVPN overlays using VXLAN, NVGRE, and MPLS over GRE. RFC 9746 later updated it.

today: RFC 8365 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 9746. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: EVPN for Shared Data-Center Networks
sections.content:
RFC 8365 specifies how Ethernet VPN (EVPN) can act as a network virtualization overlay. Its setting is a multi-tenant data center where traffic must remain separated even though tenants share the physical IP network.

The document covers VXLAN, Network Virtualization using Generic Routing Encapsulation (NVGRE), and MPLS over GRE. It also defines EVPN procedures for single-homed and multihomed network virtualization edges.
sections.plainLanguage: Several tenants can use the same physical data-center network while keeping their traffic separate. This RFC explains how EVPN carries that traffic through different kinds of IP tunnels.

sections.title: EVPN Features Used by the Overlay
sections.content:
EVPN distributes control information through Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) and learns Media Access Control (MAC) and Internet Protocol (IP) addresses in the control plane. It can use route reflectors, automatic discovery, route targets, and multicast trees or ingress replication to reduce configuration and flooding.

EVPN also supports multihoming: a customer device can connect through multiple provider edges. A single route withdrawal can remove a failed edge as a next hop for many MAC addresses, a process called mass withdrawal.
sections.plainLanguage: EVPN shares address and reachability information through Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) instead of relying only on traffic flooding. It also lets a device use more than one network connection and can signal a failure for many addresses at once.

sections.title: Tunnel Encapsulations and Virtual Identifiers
sections.content:
Virtual Extensible LAN (VXLAN) carries a 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI) in its tunnel header. Network Virtualization using Generic Routing Encapsulation (NVGRE) carries a Virtual Subnet Identifier (VSID) in the Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) key field. For route construction, this RFC uses the MPLS label fields in EVPN routes to carry the VNI or VSID.

MPLS over GRE carries the EVPN MPLS layer through an Internet Protocol (IP) tunnel, so EVPN procedures remain unchanged. An EVPN route also advertises the tunnel encapsulation type. If two network edges support several encapsulations, they can communicate only when they share at least one compatible choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tunnel packet carries an identifier for the tenant network it belongs to. EVPN advertises which tunnel type a network edge can use, so a sender can choose an option supported at both ends.

sections.title: Multihoming and Local Bias
sections.content:
In an all-active multihomed segment, more than one network edge can forward traffic. With VXLAN or NVGRE, there is no MPLS ESI label for split-horizon filtering, so the RFC recommends Local Bias.

Under Local Bias, an edge tracks the IP addresses of other edges sharing a segment. It filters multi-destination frames arriving from one of those edges on the shared segment, while the ingress edge replicates flooded traffic locally to its attached segments.
sections.plainLanguage: When several network edges connect to one segment, a frame must not loop back to the same segment. Local Bias uses the tunnel's source address to identify traffic that should be filtered.

sections.title: Multicast and Data-Center Interconnection
sections.content:
EVPN Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag routes help network edges discover multicast tunnels for an EVPN instance. The route carries tunnel information, while the encapsulation community identifies the tunnel type. For VXLAN and NVGRE, the RFC allows tunnel types for PIM trees and ingress replication.

For data-center interconnection, gateways can terminate and process EVPN routes between a data center and a WAN. An alternative uses autonomous system border routers that rewrite BGP next hops. That rewrite prevents remote edges from using per-Ethernet-segment mass withdrawal, so the procedure falls back to per-EVI withdrawal.
sections.plainLanguage: EVPN advertises how network edges can exchange multicast traffic. Between data centers, a gateway or border router can connect the networks; the border-router design uses a slower, per-instance failure update in some multihomed cases.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The security considerations for the IP tunnel technologies also apply. Changing information used to build tunnel headers or choose a tunnel can cause packets to be misrouted, delivered to the wrong place, or dropped. BGP security considerations also apply.

RFC 8365 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 9746. It has not been obsoleted according to the batch metadata.
sections.plainLanguage: If route or tunnel information is changed, traffic can be misdirected or lost. RFC 9746 later updated this Proposed Standard.
